prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration: it is now B024 alone, Katori and Ye, and I drop B019 as a second part. The reason is the attribution problem I flagged myself in round 1, and the round-1 exchange has shown that nobody can resolve it from what is in front of us. Five of the other seven members say a single name for IceCube cannot be defended, Pearce, who supports B019, says it should be the first part dropped, and no one has proposed a supportable multi-name credit. As Secretary I know that we choose the discovery first and the people second, but the people must be right, and I will not put forward a part I cannot defend name by name. B024 is what remains, and it stands on its own. Magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms is a distinct idea from the comb and from single-ion control. It produced a measurement that nature answers back to: independent clocks agreeing at the 1e-18 level, centimetre-scale gravitational redshift, and sharper limits on varying constants and on ultralight dark matter. That is the kind of clue from nature I want a prize to rest on. It also has the broadest support in the room, from four first-round configurations, and it is the common fallback of the B020 supporters, which tells me it is the position most colleagues can accept after real scientific argument.
statement.case_against: The lineage objection is not answered and I should not pretend it is. The 2005 and 2012 citations already cover the comb and the control of single quantum systems, and a critic can say the lattice clock is an excellent instrument built on honoured foundations. My answer is that the concept of trapping thousands of neutral atoms without a light shift is a new discovery in the sense that it removed a trade-off between atom number and systematics, but that is an argument and not a proof, and no one has set it against the actual 2005 and 2012 citation texts. The credit has a tail as well (SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others, and Ye's share resting partly on record performance), and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Finally, by giving up B019 I give up a real discovery of a new observational window, and I am uneasy that a good year for neutrino astronomy goes unrecognised only because of how the credit would fall.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B024 plus B019 but says B019 should be dropped first if Halzen alone cannot be defended, and asks whether the citation should name the instrument instead.
responses.response: I have moved to your own fallback. Naming the instrument does not rescue the credit, because the Nobel Prize goes to persons and the statutes leave us at three, so an instrument citation with one living name just restates the problem. The shortlist gives us Halzen and nobody else, and I will not invent names from memory to fill the gap, which is the same discipline you apply when you decline to add uncredited names. Where I still disagree with you is on the cost of a split prize: I no longer think that pairing atomic metrology with neutrino astronomy is the problem, but without a clean credit the pairing weakens B024 rather than strengthening it. I would like IceCube to come back in a later year with a record that supports a defensible attribution.

responses.point: Kroll says the lattice clock is a discovery in the sense that a measurement changed what can be measured, with a compact credit, and wants the 2005 and 2012 overlap addressed explicitly.
responses.response: I agree and I will address it, since you asked for it. The comb counts the optical cycles and the ion clock showed what control of one quantum system can do, while the lattice clock addresses a separate limit, which is how many atoms one can interrogate without a first-order Stark shift. I also repeat my request for an outside expert check of the 1e-18 comparisons and the priority of the magic-wavelength proposal, because you, Eva Lindroth and I all say we rely on memory. I take your point about your year in Hall's laboratory and your report of no collaboration with Katori or Ye as a disclosure and not a bar, though I would like the committee to record it. I do not think the credit is quite as clean as the chair says, but two names is the best available for this achievement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B020 as the whole prize because a quantitative theory preceded an unexpected experiment, but accepts that B024 is the more mature alternative and says the IceCube credit is decisive against B019.
responses.response: Your agreement on the IceCube attribution is part of why I have dropped it. On B020 I am closer to you than my round 1 suggested: a continuum model that predicts the magic angle before nature confirms it is a prediction I trust, and that is why I list it as an alternative. My hesitation is about timing and not about doubt that the phenomenon is real. The pairing mechanism is unresolved, Yuan Cao led the first experiments and stands outside the three names, and the earlier band-structure work is uncredited. If the committee judges that those questions are not settled, a prize on twisted bilayer graphene would more safely wait. If the committee wanted a different second part some day I would be glad to see it, but I do not think that it should be this year.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B051 to B020, on the ground that a transparent model predicted flat bands that nature then confirmed, and notes that the field is eight years old with an unresolved mechanism.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved from your own opening choice after reading the others, which is the honest thing and I did the same for IceCube. I find your B020 argument stronger than my round-1 comment on B051 let on, because it is a result that nature answers. Where we still differ is on how young a field a prize can sit on. You say the phenomenology is secure while the pairing is debated; I say that is true but the credit around Cao and the earlier theorists is not yet something we can defend. If B024 fails, I would turn to B020 before any other candidate, and I would take your reading of the quantitative reproducibility over mine.

responses.point: Olsson keeps B020 and names B024 as the fallback, and says that if the credit cannot be shown to be right then the better-documented B024 is the choice.
responses.response: That is the criterion I am using too. A prize should go where the credit can be shown, and for that reason B024 and not B020 is my first choice today. I also want to thank you for the frank case on IceCube, since your eighth-place ranking turned out to point at the problem the committee could not solve. On your question of what B020 would need, I would look for three things: a stable account of the pairing, evidence of reproducibility across many samples with twist-angle disorder controlled, and a settled view on the credit for Cao and the earlier theorists. If those are met the case becomes strong.

uncertainties: Whether the 1e-18 clock comparisons and the priority of the magic-wavelength proposal hold up against an external expert report, since several of us, myself included, rely on recollection.

Whether the lattice clock is judged a distinct discovery from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or an excellent instrument in an honoured lineage, and whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given the contributions of SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others, and the extent to which Ye's credit rests on record performance rather than the original idea.
Whether IceCube might later receive a defensible multi-name credit, and whether the unresolved origin of most of the diffuse flux matters for maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My supervisor David Gross and co-author Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any shortlisted candidate. As a co-opted member and Secretary, my voting status is not documented, and I flag that again. I note Kroll's disclosure of his year in John Hall's laboratory and Johansson's field overlap with B042, and I have no objection to either being recorded. I am not in the atomic, astroparticle, or condensed-matter fields of the candidates on my final list.
